Consult Summary:
- 26-year-old male with 3 hours of chest tightness, wheeze, shortness of breath and persistent cough following a recent upper respiratory tract infection.
- Assessment consistent with acute asthma exacerbation on background of chronic asthma; plan to prescribe inhalers, a spacer, and a short course of oral corticosteroids with safety advice and return precautions.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Acute asthma exacerbation
- Presentation: 3 hours of chest tightness, wheeze, non-productive cough, mild shortness of breath; worse with exertion (stairs) but not short of breath at rest.
- Timeline/progression: Symptoms began approximately 3 hours prior to consultation; cough persisted after a cold last week.
- Systems review: Associated recent sore throat and runny nose from preceding cold; no chest pain, no haemoptysis reported.
- Examination findings: No formal vital signs or physical exam documented; no peak flow available.
- Clinical impression: Physician states this is likely an asthma exacerbation related to recent viral upper respiratory tract infection.
- Management given: Prescription to be sent for inhalers (Clenil Modulite and Salbutamol/Ventolin) and a spacer; oral corticosteroid tablets prescribed for 5 days with instruction “two tablets in the morning” (steroid name not documented); advice to use Clenil daily and Ventolin as needed; if Ventolin use becomes more frequent than every 3 hours or symptoms worsen (increasing shortness of breath, chest pain, light-headedness) seek urgent medical attention.

Issue 2: Recent upper respiratory tract infection (viral cold)
- Presentation: Recent cold last week with sore throat and runny nose; symptoms improved but cough and wheeze persisted.
- Timeline/progression: Cold started last week; runny nose improving; cough persisted leading to current wheeze/asthma flare.
- Relevant negatives/positives: Cough is non-productive; no fever reported in transcript.
- Management: Supportive; treated indirectly by asthma management above.

Issue 3: Inadequate inhaler availability / recent non-adherence
- Issue: Patient reports running out of both inhalers while away at university about one week ago and has not had inhalers available during that time.
- Social context: Was away at university last week and forgot to obtain replacements.
- Impact: Likely contributed to current exacerbation per history.
- Plan: Immediate prescriptions for inhalers and a spacer; patient advised on inhaler and spacer use; return precautions and follow-up if symptoms worsen.

Medications:
- Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Clenil Modulite (beclometasone inhaler) — dose/route/frequency not documented; advised as daily controller.
- Oral corticosteroid tablets — name not documented; prescribed for 5 days, two tablets in the morning (steroid name and tablet strength not documented).
- Spacer device to be provided; instructions to be included.

Allergies:
- No drug allergies reported.
- Environmental allergies: dust (history of hay fever).

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (history of severe exacerbation in adolescence requiring intubation and hospital admission at age ~16–17).
- Childhood eczema.
- Childhood milk protein allergy.

Social History:
- Student (away at university recently).
- Lives away from home at times (implied by being at university).
- Smoking status: not mentioned.
- Alcohol use: not mentioned.
- Occupation/employment: not explicitly stated; doctor offered time off work and patient said he could self-certify first seven days.

Preventative History:
- No information documented regarding cervical screening, mammogram, prostate testing, fecal occult blood test, bone density, vaccinations, optometry, or skin checks.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs recorded.
- No physical examination findings documented.
- No peak expiratory flow measurement available.

Plan:
- Send prescriptions within the hour for:
  - Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler.
  - Clenil Modulite (beclometasone) inhaler.
  - Oral corticosteroid tablets for 5 days (two tablets each morning) — steroid name/strength to be specified on prescription.
  - Spacer device with usage instructions.
- Advise Clenil daily as controller; Ventolin PRN for wheeze; seek medical attention if Ventolin required more frequently than every 3 hours or if worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, light-headedness, or other concerning symptoms.
- Rest and consider time off work (patient may self-certify first 7 days).
- Provide spacer instructions and counsel regarding steroid side effects; advise reading medication labels.
- No immediate further investigations documented in transcript; arrange medical review if deterioration.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but expected elements:
  - Vital signs (respiratory rate, heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, blood pressure) not recorded.
  - Physical examination findings (respiratory auscultation) not recorded.
  - Peak expiratory flow (PEF) not measured.
  - Name and strength of oral corticosteroid not documented.
  - Specific inhaler doses and inhalation technique observed/documented absent.
  - Smoking, alcohol, and full occupational details not documented.
  - No explicit follow-up appointment or timeframe recorded.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - No clear internal clinical conflicts noted.
- Transcript quality:
  - Generally clear; brief audio dropout noted by both parties during discussion of steroid history/side effects.
